Feasibility trial

Pairing heat and air-quality sensors along a walking route

A first test of whether an iButton temperature logger, which has no positioning of its own, can be joined to an AirBeam air-quality monitor using timestamps alone — so that every reading of particulate pollution also carries a temperature, a humidity and a location.

One collector ran, the other walked — which is why the two sessions differ in length. The GPS traces confirm it: set 1 moved at a median 5.0 km/h with bursts reaching 9.4 km/h sustained over a full minute, and spent 17.5% of its time above 6.5 km/h. Set 2 held a steady 4.6 km/h, never exceeding 6.5 km/h for more than about 1% of the walk, and stood still for 7% of it. Worth noting for the record that set 1's running was intermittent rather than sustained — the median pace is still a brisk walk.
Matching

How much of the data paired up

The AirBeam records roughly once per second and the iButton once per minute, so each AirBeam reading takes the nearest iButton reading within 30 seconds. This table is the result of that join for each set.

“Exact to the second” counts the minutes where an iButton reading shared a timestamp with an AirBeam reading before any tolerance was allowed. The rest matched within 30 seconds. No drift correction was applied to either set.

Was anything missing?

Two separate questions: whether either instrument dropped readings, and why the temperature and humidity traces do not span quite the same width as PM2.5.

SetSession lengthAirBeam readings Seconds not recordedDropoutsLongest dropout iButton readingsiButton gaps
Set 1 3,719 s3,68336 s (1.0%) 362 s1750
Set 2 4,920 s4,771149 s (3.0%) 13112 s1740
The iButtons lost nothing. Both logged continuously at exactly 60-second intervals with no gap anywhere — 175 and 174 readings across nearly three hours.
The AirBeams did drop short stretches. Set 1 missed 36 seconds across the hour, in gaps of one or two seconds, which is negligible. Set 2 missed 149 seconds — 3% of its session — spread over 131 gaps, the longest a 12-second break at 08:15:32. Nothing was lost in the join: these seconds were never recorded in the first place. It is a small loss here, but it is exactly the failure mode that goes unnoticed in the field, which is why confirming the AirBeam is still streaming is one of the recommendations below.
Every iButton reading is accounted for. Logger 28 recorded 175 readings from 07:16 to 10:10 and logger 29 recorded 174 from 07:15 to 10:08 — continuously, every 60 seconds, with no gap anywhere. Of those, 62 and 82 fall inside their AirBeam session and every one is plotted on the maps and in the charts exactly as recorded, and counted in the summary figures and the colour scales. Nothing is filtered out.
The readings outside the session cannot be mapped. Logger 28 took 34 readings between 07:16 and 07:49 before its AirBeam started, and 79 more between 08:52 and 10:10 after it stopped. Logger 29 took 25 beforehand (07:15 – 07:39) and 67 afterwards (09:02 – 10:08). The iButton has no positioning of its own, so a reading taken while the AirBeam was not recording has no coordinate to be placed at — that is the whole dependency this trial was testing. Those readings are not lost: they are in the full record below and in every downloadable file. The temperature and humidity panels in each set section therefore begin at the first minute mark inside the AirBeam window, not at the moment the logger was switched on.

The complete logger record

Every reading either logger took, from switch-on to collection. The shaded band is the AirBeam session — the only part that can be geolocated. Note the pronounced peaks before departure and again around collection, when the loggers were not yet, or no longer, sitting undisturbed in the open air.

Method

Two instruments, joined on time

Nothing connects the two devices in the field. Each writes its own timestamped log, and the two logs are joined afterwards in Python.

Pair the devicesEach iButton is assigned to one specific AirBeam and recorded as a fixed pairing, so the two streams can never be crossed in processing.
Log with marginThe iButtons log from well before the walk until well after it, so the AirBeam session sits entirely inside the iButton window.
Cover the routeEach collector carries one set around the campus loop — one running, one walking.
Join on timestampEvery AirBeam reading takes the nearest iButton reading within 30 seconds, giving each position a temperature and humidity.
Flag, don't deleteHandling artefacts and GPS spikes are marked with quality flags so they can be excluded from analysis while the raw record survives.
Important caveat about this trial. The two devices were not set to a single reference clock before this run. The match still came out at 100%, which tells us the clocks happened to be close enough over a session of about an hour — but that is luck, not method. For the actual campaign the clocks must be set deliberately from one source, which is the first recommendation below. Without that step there is no guarantee that a temperature is pinned to the right place, and at walking pace even a two-minute discrepancy puts a reading roughly 150 m from where it was taken.

Next

Recommendations for the actual run

The trial shows the method works. These are the things to fix or decide before collecting data that will be used for analysis.

Priority

Set both devices to the same clock

This was not done in the trial. Program every iButton from one machine, synced to network time, and confirm the AirCasting phone is on network time on the same morning. Record the programming time in the field log. Everything downstream depends on this one step.

Priority

Match route length to iButton memory

Work out the distance and duration to be covered before setting the logging interval. The DS1923 holds a fixed number of readings, so a long route at a short interval fills the memory mid-session and the tail of the walk is lost. Calculate it once and write it into the protocol: duration in minutes divided by the interval must stay under the capacity.

Priority

One person carries both devices

The AirBeam's GPS is the only source of position, so the iButton must travel with it exactly. Two carriers means the temperature is pinned to the wrong person's location. Both devices on the same mount, on the same body.

Priority

Check the AirBeam is still recording

The AirBeam can drop its connection mid-session without any obvious signal to the carrier. Agree a fixed check interval — every 10 minutes, say — where the collector confirms the app is still streaming, and log each check. A dropout discovered afterwards cannot be recovered.

Decide

Choose walking or running, and be consistent

The two modes are not interchangeable. Running covers more ground but gives the iButton less time to settle at each point, and this trial shows why that matters: once the loggers had settled, the temperature spread across the rest of the route was only 1.0–1.5 °C, far less than the real difference between sunlit road and shaded path. The sealed steel case responds over minutes, not seconds. Walking is the better choice for heat; if the campaign needs running, the heat data should be treated as a route-level average rather than a street-level measurement.

Add

Use a deliberate sync marker

At the start and end of each route, warm the iButton in a closed hand for a minute and note the clock time. That leaves a sharp, identifiable spike in the trace at a known moment, so alignment can be proved from the data instead of assumed — cheap insurance if a clock does drift.

Add

Shield the iButton and keep it off the body

Both units recorded sharp excursions at the same three moments — before departure, at the start of the route, and around collection, reaching 34.06 °C at 07:33. Readings that high are not plausible for Lagos air at that hour, so the loggers were measuring something other than the open air. Mount the logger in a ventilated radiation shield at breathing height, on a strap or boom clear of the carrier, give it several minutes to settle before the route begins, and keep a short field log of when the devices are touched, so these moments are recorded rather than inferred.

Add

Calibrate the loggers as a batch

Before and after the campaign, sit every iButton side by side in one place for an hour and compare. That gives a known offset per unit instead of an assumed one. The two units in this trial tracked each other to within about half a degree, which is encouraging, but it is a comparison between two sensors rather than against a reference.

Add

Allow the GPS to settle before starting

Set 1 produced 29 position spikes, one implying 75.6 m/s, which inflated its route by half a kilometre before filtering. Stand still for a minute or two until the fix is stable, then begin. Keep the 4 m/s filter in the pipeline either way.

Add

Repeat routes at different times of day

A single pass records a moment, not a place. Repeating the same segments at dawn, midday and evening is what separates a hot street from a hot hour, and it is the only way the data supports a claim about a location.

Data

The underlying files

All four files are embedded in this page, so it works as a single self-contained document with nothing else alongside it.

Column reference

The cleaned paired file: one row per AirBeam reading with its matched iButton values.

ColumnMeaningSource
pair_id28 or 29 — which setPairing log
timestampLocal time, Africa/Lagos (UTC+1)AirBeam
latitude, longitudePosition of the reading, decimal degreesAirBeam GPS
pm1, pm25, pm10_air_ug_m3Particulate concentrations, µg/m³AirBeam
temperature_ibutton_cAir temperature, °C, nearest reading within 30 siButton
humidity_ibutton_pctRelative humidity, %, same matchiButton
step_speedImplied speed from the previous fix, m/sDerived
gps_okFalse where implied speed exceeds 4 m/s — a position spikeDerived
heat_okCarried through from the source export; not applied in this report — every reading is shown and counted as recordedSource export
Rows are kept, never deleted. The only filter applied to the figures on this page is gps_ok, which removes implausible position jumps from the route geometry. Every temperature and humidity reading is shown and counted exactly as the logger recorded it. The AirBeam's own temperature and humidity channels are present in the original export but were not used in this analysis — all heat and humidity figures here come from the iButtons.
